attacker_roles: Unauthenticated web client or visitor in a Discord channel
Authenticated dashboard user / owner acting concurrently
Configured Discord administrator making an accidental destructive action
Malicious or compromised Minecraft server selected by an authorized operator
On-path network actor for a misconfigured transport topology
Local/CI workspace attacker able to alter untracked Docker-context artifacts
key_invariants: A token reissue must invalidate every prior bearer credential for that user.
Only public, policy-approved network destinations may be connected to absent an exact configured exception.
Untrusted runtime input cannot cause unbounded durable/stream buffering or terminate the whole process.
Per-user/global bot quotas must hold across concurrent creation requests.
A lifecycle timeout/terminal event must not leave stale work or double-charge reconnect state.
Discord output and destructive confirmation must be scoped to the intended viewer/message/target.
Remote database and public dashboard transport must preserve confidentiality and peer validation.
The built runtime image must contain only reviewed/allowlisted application artifacts.

findings.title: Unhandled async event-boundary failures can deliberately terminate the entire service
findings.symbol: Discord event listener registration (combined event-boundary finding)
findings.root_cause: Two independent external event boundaries invoke asynchronous work without owning/catching its Promise: the Discord client wrapper discards every event.execute Promise, and stateChange discards critical Persistence.updateBotState. The top-level unhandledRejection policy then intentionally shuts down the entire process. In Discord.js, an uncaught listener rejection is surfaced as an unhandled Client error when no error listener is installed.
findings.violated_invariant: A malformed/failed external event or transient persistence error must not make every bot, dashboard endpoint, and control-plane process exit.
findings.data_flow: Discord autocomplete or ready event -> src/discord/client.js raw listener -> rejected async event.execute -> Discord Client error/unhandled rejection -> index.js crashExit -> process.exit(1). Separately: BotInstance stateChange -> instanceEvents.attachInstanceEvents -> rejected Persistence.updateBotState critical write -> unhandledRejection -> same crashExit.
attack_scenario: A transient database failure coincides with a bot state transition, causing the critical persistence Promise to reject after the synchronous EventEmitter callback returns.
Or an administrator invokes autocomplete while its token metadata database operation rejects; interactionCreate awaits it outside its command-error catch.

The rejection is not contained at its event boundary. The process-level handler begins shutdown and exits non-zero, taking down all bots and the dashboard; a process manager can restart into a repeat failure loop.
findings.attacker_role: Malicious Minecraft server influencing state transitions, or a legitimate Discord administrator exercising autocomplete during a dependency failure.
findings.preconditions: A reachable external event plus a rejected persistence/autocomplete/ready Promise; no production service was contacted for this audit.
findings.affected_deployment: Every single-process deployment; impact is amplified when a restart manager retries immediately.

impact.integrity: In-flight lifecycle persistence may be interrupted or compensated inconsistently.
impact.availability: High: one rejected event can stop the entire Node process and all supervised bots.
impact.blast_radius: Whole process, dashboard, Discord control plane, and every managed bot.
impact.business_impact: A hostile server or ordinary dependency outage can produce fleet-wide downtime rather than isolated degraded behavior.

reproduction.type: local mocked Discord and persistence rejection probes; no Discord, database, or Minecraft service contacted
steps: Loaded the current Discord event wrapper with a synthetic autocomplete command that rejects and an audit-only Client error observer.
Emitted a local synthetic interaction. The discarded listener rejection became a Client error; without the observer, the child process exited code 1.
Independently replaced the persistence state write with a rejected Promise and emitted a local stateChange; the promise had no listener-side catch and reached the configured unhandled-rejection path.
reproduction.expected_result: The event boundary logs/metrics the failure, preserves a defined degraded state, and the process remains alive.
reproduction.observed_result: The current listener patterns discard the promises; the Discord mock produced the unhandled Client-error behavior and the persistence path has the same uncaught Promise shape.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Mocks/fakes only; values and output contained no real credentials or identifiers.

findings.existing_controls: Mineflayer event handlers have a local makeGuard, command execution for chat-input interactions has a try/catch, and Persistence recovers its internal write chain. Neither control wraps the two failing boundaries above. index.js deliberately exits on unhandled rejection.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Wrap every loaded Discord event with Promise.resolve(event.execute(...args)).catch(reportEventFailure) and register a nonfatal, redacted client error listener. In attachInstanceEvents, explicitly void/catch updateBotState and enter a measurable retry/degraded-persistence policy rather than allowing a rejection to escape.
alternatives: Introduce a shared async EventEmitter/listener wrapper used by Discord, BotInstance, timers, and SSE listeners.
Serialize state persistence through a retry queue with bounded backoff and alert only after durable failure thresholds.
regression_tests: Reject autocomplete and ready handlers; assert no unhandledRejection, Client error crash, or process exit.
Reject updateBotState from stateChange; assert rejection is observed/recorded and later writes can recover.
Assert a Client error listener itself cannot recursively throw.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: All external async listeners have a defined rejection sink; an injected rejected handler leaves the process alive and emits only redacted operational telemetry.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Adding catch wrappers is narrow, but persistence retry/degraded-state policy must be agreed to avoid silently accepting lost durable state.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The command try/catch does not cover autocomplete (lines 12-18), client.js does not return/await the promise, and instanceEvents has no catch. The local Discord mock demonstrated the actual library error behavior rather than assuming generic EventEmitter semantics.
findings.limitations: No real Discord gateway or PostgreSQL endpoint was contacted; behavior was demonstrated with local controlled mocks and source review.

findings.title: Dashboard token reissue is deterministic within a second and renewal usually rejects its own calculated TTL
findings.root_cause: JWT payloads contain only userId and library-generated second-resolution timestamps, with no jti/random claim. Equal user/TTL requests in one Unix second generate the identical HMAC token and hash, so the UPSERT cannot invalidate the prior bearer. Renewal derives an arbitrary millisecond difference then passes it to a validator that requires exact whole seconds.
findings.violated_invariant: Replacing a bearer token must always create a distinct credential and invalidate the prior credential; a documented renewal must produce a valid token for a valid stored session.
findings.data_flow: Administrator Discord/API token request -> issueToken/issueTokenDays -> deterministic jwt.sign payload -> SHA-256 hash -> web_tokens UPSERT -> cookie/API authentication. Renewal reads expires_at -> calculateRenewedExpiry preserves milliseconds -> ttlMs subtracts current milliseconds -> signToken rejects non-multiple-of-1000 duration.
attack_scenario: An administrator attempts to rotate/reissue a user token quickly using the same day lifetime after suspecting it was exposed.
Both requests occur in the same second and produce the same bearer/hash. The database update and auth:revoked event happen, but a holder of the supposed old token can continue authenticating.
Separately, a normal renewal derives a millisecond TTL and returns an error instead of extending access, encouraging insecure manual workarounds or unexpected session expiry.
findings.attacker_role: A prior bearer-token holder or an administrator/user affected by normal renewal.
findings.preconditions: For reissue, same user, same TTL, and two requests in one Unix second. For renewal, a valid stored token with ordinary millisecond timestamps.
findings.affected_deployment: Any dashboard deployment using token reissue or renewal.

impact.confidentiality: A token intended to be replaced can remain usable by a prior holder.
impact.integrity: Prior holder retains dashboard actions permitted to that user.
impact.availability: Renewal fails for normal timestamps, disrupting administration.
impact.blast_radius: The affected dashboard user and any bots they own; admin sessions if the token belongs to an administrator.
impact.business_impact: Emergency token rotation is unreliable, and normal credential maintenance fails unexpectedly.

reproduction.type: local pure-function deterministic proof; no database or network connection
steps: Loaded tokenService with audit-only dummy configuration and signed two same-user, same-TTL tokens in the same process/second.
Calculated a renewed expiry from a timestamp containing milliseconds and tested its derived TTL with the production whole-second validator.
reproduction.expected_result: Reissued tokens differ and each valid day renewal passes signing validation.
reproduction.observed_result: sameSecondIssueTokensIdentical=true; tokenPayloadHasJti=false; calculated renewal TTL was rejected because its modulo one second was nonzero. Raw tokens were never printed.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No token, secret, DB row, or external endpoint was emitted or contacted.

findings.existing_controls: HS256 is pinned during verification, active hashes are checked against PostgreSQL, expiry is checked, and tests cover TTL helper bounds. Tests do not cover same-second reissue uniqueness or renewToken using a real calculated TTL.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Generate a cryptographically random jti for every issuance/renewal and include it in the signed payload. Derive issued_at/expires_at from a canonical integer-second clock, store/return that canonical expiration, and sign the exact integer-second duration.
alternatives: Store a random session identifier alongside the hash and require it during verification.
Use opaque random server-side session tokens rather than self-contained JWTs.
regression_tests: Issue identical user/TTL tokens repeatedly under a fixed same-second clock and assert different raw token/hash each time.
Verify the first token fails after the second is stored.
Renew an expiry with nonzero milliseconds and assert a valid canonical token/result.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Every issuance has unique entropy, reissue invalidates every prior bearer immediately, and valid 1–365-day renewals always return a token with a whole-second expiry.

findings.auto_fix_reason: The scope is contained in token generation/renewal with clear deterministic regression cases, though a deployment migration should preserve currently active sessions intentionally.
findings.false_positive_analysis: jsonwebtoken HMAC signing is deterministic for an identical header/payload/secret; the local proof directly observed equality. The `% 1000` validation branch and Date.now subtraction are both in the current production path.
findings.limitations: The proof used audit-only dummy signing configuration and did not invoke a real database transaction.

findings.title: Public-only Minecraft egress policy accepts special-use and IPv4-compatible IPv6 destinations
findings.root_cause: The IPv6 classifier only rejects a small set of prefixes. Deprecated site-local and IPv4-compatible IPv6 forms fall through to public=true, so assertPublicDestination accepts them without the exact-private-IP allowlist. The connector subsequently uses that accepted address as Mineflayer host.
findings.violated_invariant: Every non-public/special-use destination must be denied unless explicitly approved as an exact literal; address syntax variants must not bypass the policy.
findings.data_flow: Discord/API bot host -> validateHost -> BotManager record -> BotInstance._connect -> connector.createMineflayerBot -> assertPublicDestination -> isPublicIpv6 returns true -> mineflayer.createBot({ host: destination.address }).
attack_scenario: An authorized dashboard/Discord user supplies a syntactically valid IPv6 literal that encodes a special/local route.
The public-only classifier accepts it and no private allowlist entry is needed.
On a host/network with a route, translator, or compatibility handling for that form, Mineflayer connects to an internal/special-use target and can send its protocol traffic.
findings.attacker_role: A dashboard user or configured Discord administrator allowed to create/edit a bot destination.
findings.preconditions: A deployment IPv6/network route that can reach the accepted special-use or compatible address; no real endpoint was contacted.
findings.affected_deployment: IPv6-enabled hosts, NAT64/compatibility environments, or networks that route the accepted special-use prefix.

impact.confidentiality: Can expose network reachability/protocol responses from otherwise protected destinations.
impact.integrity: Can send Minecraft protocol traffic to unintended internal services.
impact.availability: Can consume internal connection resources or target service capacity.
impact.blast_radius: Network interfaces reachable from the bot host.
impact.business_impact: Violates the documented egress isolation and can turn bot configuration into an internal network probe.

reproduction.type: local pure-policy probe; no socket connection attempted
steps: Called isPublicIpAddress and assertPublicDestination for a deprecated site-local IPv6 literal and two IPv4-compatible IPv6 literals.
Recorded only booleans, not a network target or any response.
reproduction.expected_result: All special-use/IPv4-compatible forms are denied with Destination is not permitted.
reproduction.observed_result: Each tested form returned classifierSaysPublic=true and directDestinationAccepted=true; no network connection was attempted.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Pure local function calls only; no DNS lookup or real Minecraft/internal service access.

findings.existing_controls: IPv4 private/link-local/metadata/reserved checks, mapped IPv4 check, all-answer DNS rejection, address pinning, and exact literal allowlist are positive controls. Existing egress tests omit the demonstrated forms.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Use a vetted IP/CIDR classification library or a complete explicit denylist for IPv6 special-use ranges; normalize and detect IPv4-compatible/translated forms before declaring them public. Default-deny any category not proven globally routable.
alternatives: Permit only an explicit allowlist of public DNS names/IPs for production bots.
Add network-level egress filtering independent of application checks.
regression_tests: Add direct and DNS-returned site-local, IPv4-compatible, translated, documentation, and other special-use IPv6 cases.
Assert mixed public/special IPv6 DNS answers reject and no connector call occurs.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No special-use or IPv4-embedded private/loopback form reaches createMineflayerBot unless an explicit, normalized policy exception permits it.

findings.auto_fix_reason: IP category policy is security-sensitive and must preserve documented intentional private-server exceptions across IPv4/IPv6.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The finding does not claim every listed literal routes in every OS. It proves the application policy accepts them despite its documented denial promise; reachability is explicitly deployment-dependent.
findings.limitations: An earlier local transport check for a compatible IPv6 form returned an unroutable error in this sandbox; it is not claimed as a transport bypass. No internal network was probed.

findings.title: Untrusted runtime text reaches unredacted, unbounded durable logs and unbackpressured live SSE
findings.category: Sensitive logging and uncontrolled resource consumption
findings.owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.symbol: safeText, botLog, Pino streams, SSE bridge
findings.root_cause: The generic log path uses safeText/sanitizeForLog, which removes control characters but does not invoke redactDiagnostic or enforce a length. AuthFlow sends attacker-controlled hard-failure server text to botLog. Pino JSONL streams append forever with no rotation/retention/size/rate control, and eventHub/routes write every live log to SSE without honoring res.write backpressure.
findings.violated_invariant: Secrets and attacker-controlled diagnostics must not be retained/streamed raw, and a single bot/server/client must not make durable logs or pending stream buffers grow without a bounded policy.
findings.data_flow: Minecraft server message -> botEventBinder.onServerMessage -> AuthFlow.onHardFail(message) -> botLog -> safeText only -> Pino stdout/combined.jsonl/error.jsonl + in-memory buffer + eventHub -> owner REST/SSE. Error/warn summaries later reach Discord through redactDiagnostic, but that does not retroactively protect JSONL/SSE.
attack_scenario: A malicious Minecraft server receives the bot authentication command, then emits repeated hard-failure messages that include a secret-shaped or arbitrary payload.
The message is logged at error level without redaction and is retained in host/container logs and delivered to a slow owner SSE client.
Repeated messages grow append-only log files and unconsumed response buffers, exhausting disk/memory or exposing echoed sensitive data to log readers.
findings.attacker_role: A malicious/compromised Minecraft server selected by an authorized user; a slow authenticated SSE consumer can amplify queued response memory.
findings.preconditions: A bot connects and reaches AUTHENTICATING, or another untrusted runtime diagnostic reaches botLog; log volume is writable.
findings.affected_deployment: All long-running deployments with durable LOG_DIR output; Docker bind/volume logging amplifies host disk impact.

impact.confidentiality: Sensitive values echoed in untrusted diagnostics can persist in JSONL/stdout/SSE despite redaction expectations.
impact.integrity: Logs/audit context become attacker-influenced and misleading.
impact.availability: Unlimited append-only files and ignored SSE backpressure can consume disk or memory.
impact.blast_radius: Host log volume, process memory, dashboard log viewers, and operational log aggregation.
impact.business_impact: Can leak credentials into operational systems and cause broad service instability through resource exhaustion.

reproduction.type: local module mock and static sink proof; no network/log contents read
steps: Replaced botLog in an isolated child module graph with a capture stub, then called AuthFlow.onHardFail with an audit-only marker in a synthetic server message.
Recorded booleans only; the marker itself was never printed or written into the audit artifact.
Reviewed stream mode and SSE write code statically.
reproduction.expected_result: The marker is redacted or omitted before botLog, and durable/live paths have explicit bounded retention/backpressure behavior.
reproduction.observed_result: hardFailClassified=true, logLevel=error, unredactedMarkerReachedLogSink=true, redactionAppliedBeforeLogSink=false. Both file streams are append-mode and SSE ignores write return values.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Local fake logger and temporary outside-repository log directory only. Existing runtime log contents were deliberately not read.

findings.existing_controls: Ring buffers cap per-bot/summary memory; DiscordNotifier calls redactDiagnostic; control characters and ANSI are filtered; Docker code directory is read-only. None applies secrecy redaction/retention/backpressure to the Pino message/file/SSE path. README currently describes rotating logs although no rotation exists.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Treat all untrusted server/error text as redactDiagnostic(message).slice(maxBytes) before botLog, and log stable error categories rather than arbitrary remote text. Add a configured rotating/retained log sink with file-size/total-disk limits and a bounded SSE queue that pauses/coalesces/drops log events when res.write returns false.
alternatives: Use platform log rotation with strict volume quota plus an application-side message cap.
Separate privileged raw diagnostics from dashboard-visible sanitized events and require explicit opt-in secure retention.
regression_tests: Inject a marker through hard-fail/kick/error paths and assert absent from Pino capture, REST logs, SSE, and Discord summary.
Simulate a false-returning SSE write and assert bounded queue/drop/coalesce behavior.
Assert file rotation/retention limit under a temporary local volume.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No raw untrusted diagnostic reaches durable/dashboard logs, every log message is size-bounded, and sustained output cannot exceed configured disk or pending-SSE budgets.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Redacting this path is straightforward, but retention, drop behavior, and incident-forensics requirements need an operator-approved policy.
findings.false_positive_analysis: redactDiagnostic is a different function used by DiscordNotifier, not botLog. The local capture proves the source marker survives safeText. Bounded in-memory buffers do not bound fs.createWriteStream append files or HTTP response write queues.
findings.limitations: No production log was opened and no disk-exhaustion load test was performed. Exact disk/memory rate depends on Minecraft message rate, log aggregation, and client network speed.

findings.title: Bot quota checks race across concurrent asynchronous creation requests
findings.root_cause: Per-owner and global count checks use the in-memory map before an awaited persistence operation. Multiple requests can all observe capacity, persist serially, and each register afterward. No database transaction/reservation constrains the count.
findings.violated_invariant: Configured global and per-owner bot limits must remain true under concurrent requests, not merely sequential calls.
findings.data_flow: Authenticated owner API/Discord create request -> BotManager.createBot -> in-memory count check -> awaited Persistence.saveBotWithActivity transaction -> _register adds to Map -> published snapshot. Concurrent calls pass the check before either registration.
attack_scenario: A user at one slot below their configured limit sends two or more valid create requests concurrently.
Each invocation sees the same old in-memory count and passes rate/quota checks.
After the gated persistence operations resolve, each call registers a bot; resource/memory/network limits are exceeded.
findings.attacker_role: Authenticated dashboard user or configured Discord administrator able to create bots.
findings.preconditions: Remaining capacity and two or more concurrent valid creation requests; process-local creation limiter still permits the burst.
findings.affected_deployment: All deployments; multi-replica deployments need cross-process protection as well.

impact.availability: Extra bot instances consume memory, connections, CPU, and potentially account/server quotas.
impact.blast_radius: Per-owner and global fleet capacity, depending on the race position.
impact.business_impact: A user can overrun resource/cost controls and destabilize the shared bot supervisor.

reproduction.type: local concurrency mock with no database/network side effect
steps: Seeded the manager with four synthetic records under a limit of five.
Held two mocked Persistence.saveBotWithActivity calls at a barrier after both passed the production count checks.
Released both and counted registered records.
reproduction.expected_result: At most one request succeeds and final owner count remains five.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Persistence/register/audit effects were in-memory stubs; no bot, DB, Discord, or network call occurred.

findings.existing_controls: Per-user sliding-window creation limits, an in-memory global count, and a DB unique host/port/username constraint help but do not serialize capacity reservation. Unique account constraint does not enforce counts.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Reserve capacity atomically in PostgreSQL (for example a locked per-owner/global counter or transaction/advisory lock and count) before inserting the record; release/compensate reservation on failure.
alternatives: Use a keyed mutex only for explicitly single-process deployments.
Introduce a quota table with atomic conditional UPDATE/INSERT and metrics.
regression_tests: Barrier-test N concurrent creates from one slot below per-user limit.
Barrier-test global limit.
Test transaction failure releases a reservation and multi-process/database semantics.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No concurrent interleaving can commit/register more records than either configured quota, including across replicas.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Correct atomic reservation needs schema/transaction semantics and a clear multi-replica policy.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The mock preserves the exact production check-before-await ordering. Rate limiting is a burst control, not a mutual exclusion mechanism, and the database schema has no count constraint.
findings.limitations: No PostgreSQL instance was available; atomic SQL design must be integration-tested against the target database/version.

findings.title: Queue timeout reports failure while an uncancelled bot startup can later attach and run
findings.root_cause: Queue creates an AbortSignal on timeout, but start passes a zero-argument closure and _connect/createMineflayerBot do not receive or observe that signal. The queue rejects its caller and starts draining later work while the original DNS/connect promise continues. Its own separate abort controller remains current, so a late bot is attached.
findings.violated_invariant: A timed-out start must mean no live connection can be created later without an explicit new start request, and queued work must remain serial with any underlying operation.
findings.data_flow: Dashboard/Discord start -> BotManager.startBot -> BotInstance.start -> Queue.enqueue timeout controller -> ignored closure signal -> BotInstance._connect -> createMineflayerBot -> late resolved bot -> _bot assignment/event binding.
attack_scenario: A slow DNS/connection path to a user-configured public server exceeds BOT_QUEUE_TIMEOUT.
The caller receives a timeout and may assume the bot did not start.
The background connect resolves later and attaches a bot in CONNECTING state; subsequent operations can overlap a task believed cancelled.
findings.attacker_role: A destination server/DNS path that delays setup, or an authorized user supplying such a destination.
findings.preconditions: Connection setup takes longer than the configured queue timeout and the user does not subsequently stop/destroy the instance before the promise resolves.
findings.affected_deployment: All deployments with slow/unresponsive destination resolution/connection behavior.

impact.integrity: Operational state can contradict the reported result and later actions may overlap.
impact.availability: Unexpected bot connections consume queue, network, and account resources.
impact.blast_radius: The affected bot and shared host capacity.
impact.business_impact: Operators lose a reliable stop/start contract and may leave unwanted bots connected.

reproduction.type: local controlled connector mock; no DNS, Minecraft server, database, or Discord contact
steps: Configured a short queue timeout in an isolated child process.
Replaced createMineflayerBot before loading BotInstance with a delayed local fake EventEmitter bot.
Called start, observed timeout, waited for fake connector resolution, then inspected only state/attachment booleans and stopped the fake bot.
reproduction.expected_result: After the timeout, no late connection is attached unless a new explicit start is issued.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No socket was opened and all bot methods were local stubs.

findings.existing_controls: Queue has timeout, drain, linked AbortControllers, and BotInstance has generation/abort checks. Explicit stop/destroy aborts the instance controller, but Queue timeout uses a different unobserved controller.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Pass Queue's signal into _connect and connector resolution, invalidate the connection generation on timeout, and check signal/generation before every attach. Keep the queue blocked until underlying cancellation acknowledges or make the task operation idempotently self-terminating.
alternatives: Use one operation-scoped AbortController owned by BotInstance for both Queue and connector.
Replace Promise.race-only timeout with a cancellable connection operation that has a completion barrier.
regression_tests: Delay connector past queue timeout and assert no _bot/event listener survives.
Race timeout with stop, restart, and delete.
Assert no following queue task overlaps unresolved cancelled work.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: A timeout guarantees the attempted connection cannot become current later; stop/restart/delete races are idempotent.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Cancellation affects network/library behavior and queue sequencing; a narrow source change needs lifecycle integration testing.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The local fake follows the exact code path: Queue supplies a signal, start ignores its parameter, and _connect creates a distinct controller. Explicit stop would mitigate later attachment, but it is not automatically invoked on timeout.
findings.limitations: No real DNS or Mineflayer socket cancellation was tested; this proof intentionally avoids external services.

findings.title: One Mineflayer disconnect can consume the reconnect budget twice
findings.root_cause: Both terminal event handlers independently call handleDisconnect without a per-connection terminal guard. Mineflayer registers kicked when it receives a disconnect packet and also emits end when the underlying client ends. handleDisconnect clears/replaces the timer but increments attempts/history each invocation.
findings.violated_invariant: Each physical connection loss must cause at most one state transition, alert, and reconnect-budget charge.
findings.data_flow: Minecraft disconnect packet -> Mineflayer kicked event -> botEventBinder -> ReconnectPolicy.handleDisconnect -> _scheduleBackoff (attempt 1). Underlying socket end -> Mineflayer end event -> same handler -> _scheduleBackoff (attempt 2).
attack_scenario: A hostile or unstable Minecraft server disconnects a bot normally.
The protocol produces kicked and then end for the same connection.
The bot spends two of its five reconnect slots. Repeated normal disconnects can move it to ERROR after roughly three losses rather than the configured five.
findings.attacker_role: Malicious or unreliable Minecraft server to which the authorized operator connected a bot.
findings.preconditions: autoReconnect enabled and Mineflayer emits its normal disconnect plus underlying end sequence.
findings.affected_deployment: Every Mineflayer-backed bot with reconnect enabled.

impact.integrity: Reconnect metrics/state and operator expectations are inaccurate.
impact.availability: A remote server can force early per-bot reconnect exhaustion and outage.
impact.blast_radius: One bot per terminal connection, with shared log/alert noise.
impact.business_impact: Fleet operators see avoidable ERROR states and must manually restart bots after ordinary disconnects.

reproduction.type: local in-memory state-machine proof plus installed dependency source inspection
steps: Created a fake BotInstance and invoked ReconnectPolicy.handleDisconnect twice to model kicked then end for one connection.
Inspected the installed Mineflayer kick plugin and loader: disconnect packet emits kicked, underlying client end emits end.
Cleared the local timer without waiting for a real network connection.
reproduction.expected_result: One connection loss increments attempts/history once and arms one reconnect timer.
reproduction.observed_result: terminalEventsForOneSyntheticConnection=2, reconnectAttemptsCharged=2, historyEntriesCharged=2, with state transitions DISCONNECTED -> RECONNECTING repeated twice.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No remote Minecraft host was contacted. A separate loopback protocol-fixture attempt did not yield a kicked event before teardown and is not relied upon.

findings.existing_controls: Reconnect timer replacement limits live timers to one and alert cooldown limits messages; neither prevents the second attempt/history charge. Mineflayer event handlers are guarded for exceptions, not deduplicated for semantics.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Track a terminal-handled flag keyed to BotInstance connection generation; let the first kicked/end handler process lifecycle and make later terminal events log-only/no-op. Reset only on the next successful _connect generation.
alternatives: Make end the sole reconnect lifecycle trigger and use kicked only to retain a reason.
Use a single disconnect adapter that combines Mineflayer events before reaching ReconnectPolicy.
regression_tests: Emit kicked then end on one fake bot and assert attempts/history/timer are one.
Emit end alone and kicked alone to retain recovery.
Race terminal events with stop and restart.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Any terminal event sequence for one connection produces exactly one reconnect charge and no stale timer.

findings.auto_fix_reason: A generation-scoped idempotence guard is localized and has deterministic fake-event regression coverage.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The production handlers are distinct and state only excludes OFFLINE; after kicked, state is RECONNECTING, so end does not return. The installed dependency source explicitly registers both emissions on this disconnect path.
findings.limitations: The proof relies on the installed locked Mineflayer implementation and synthetic event order, not a live server.

findings.title: Three administrator Discord commands publish fleet details to every channel viewer
findings.root_cause: list-bot, status-bot, and stats defer normal visible responses despite rendering owner-scoped bot host/user/status/position and process/fleet data. Admin invocation authorization does not restrict subsequent message visibility to the caller.
findings.violated_invariant: Operational inventory and detailed status visible only to an authorized command actor must not be disclosed to unrelated members of the Discord channel.
findings.data_flow: Configured admin invokes slash command -> interactionCreate authorizes actor -> command resolves owner-scoped records/stats -> normal deferred Discord reply -> all members with channel visibility can read embed.
attack_scenario: A configured administrator invokes one of the affected commands in a shared Discord channel.
A non-admin channel member cannot invoke the command but can read the normal response.
The member learns bot endpoints/usernames/live state/position or process fleet/resource details useful for reconnaissance.
findings.attacker_role: Any Discord user who can view the channel where an administrator invokes the command.
findings.preconditions: Affected command used in a channel shared with an untrusted viewer.
findings.affected_deployment: Discord deployments that use non-private admin channels.

impact.confidentiality: Discloses bot inventory, endpoint/username metadata, live status/position, and fleet/process statistics.
impact.blast_radius: Up to all bots returned in list/stats and all viewers of the message channel.
impact.business_impact: Leaked infrastructure/account metadata improves targeting of bot accounts and internal services.

reproduction.type: deterministic source/API-option proof; no Discord contact
steps: Reviewed every command deferReply/reply/editReply site and compared response flags.
Confirmed the three affected commands call deferReply with no flags while their embeds render data from authorized BotManager records/stats.
Confirmed neighboring token, log, lifecycle, and help command paths use explicit ephemeral flags where intended.
reproduction.expected_result: Sensitive operational commands begin with a deferred reply carrying MessageFlags.Ephemeral.
reproduction.observed_result: Affected paths have deferReply() without flags, which Discord treats as a normal channel-visible interaction response.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Static deterministic proof only; no Discord account, guild, channel, or message was used.

findings.existing_controls: interactionCreate checks configured admin IDs and manager methods scope returned bots to the caller. logs-bot/new-token/renew-token/delete and lifecycle commands are already ephemeral, but those controls do not make a normal reply private.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Import MessageFlags and call deferReply({ flags: MessageFlags.Ephemeral }) in list-bot, status-bot, and stats; ensure all error/success edits remain tied to that deferred ephemeral interaction.
alternatives: Adopt a command-response helper that defaults all administrative responses to ephemeral and requires an explicit reviewed public opt-in.
regression_tests: Mock each affected command and assert its first deferReply receives the ephemeral flag.
Audit all command modules for an intentional public-response allowlist.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No admin command returning bot/fleet metadata can create a channel-visible response unless explicitly documented and approved.

findings.auto_fix_reason: A narrow, compatible interaction option change with deterministic mocks and no data-model migration.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Discord application command permissions gate invocation, not visibility of normal responses. No later edit can convert a non-ephemeral deferred reply into a private response.
findings.limitations: Actual channel ACLs are deployment-specific and were not inspected; the finding applies whenever a channel has an unintended viewer.

findings.title: Discord deletion confirmation collectors are not bound to the prompt message or a unique nonce
findings.excerpt:
new ButtonBuilder().setCustomId('confirm_delete')
...
filter: (i) => i.user.id === interaction.user.id &&
  ['confirm_delete', 'cancel_delete'].includes(i.customId)
...
await BotManager.deleteBot(principal, match.id);
findings.root_cause: Every deletion dialog uses the same two component IDs, and awaitMessageComponent is collected from the whole channel with a filter that checks only the clicking user and static ID. It neither checks i.message.id against the edited reply nor binds a per-dialog cryptographic nonce/target.
findings.violated_invariant: A confirmation click must authorize only the exact destructive action shown in the message that the user clicked.
findings.data_flow: Admin invokes delete for target A/B -> both channel collectors listen for same user/static component IDs -> click on one prompt satisfies all matching collectors -> each captured match.id can call BotManager.deleteBot.
attack_scenario: A permitted administrator opens two deletion prompts in the same channel before either expires.
The administrator clicks Confirm on the prompt for target B.

The earlier collector for target A also accepts the interaction. Depending on collector/interaction acknowledgment ordering, target A can be deleted or a command error is produced; the click is not cryptographically/message-bound to B.
findings.attacker_role: A configured administrator making concurrent actions; a user who can induce or race a second dialog in the same authorized session.
findings.preconditions: Two active delete dialogs for the same user in the same Discord channel within 30 seconds.

impact.integrity: Wrong bot record/configuration can be deleted.
impact.availability: Deleted bot stops and cannot operate until recreated.
impact.blast_radius: Any two simultaneously pending deletion targets for a user/channel.
impact.business_impact: A confirmation safety control can delete an unintended bot, potentially losing its encrypted account configuration.

reproduction.type: local command mock using synthetic interactions only
steps: Started two delete-bot.execute calls with different synthetic target IDs and one fake channel that captures collector filters.
Fed one synthetic button interaction identifying a second prompt to both filters.
Modeled the one-time interaction acknowledgment behavior after the first collector proceeds.
reproduction.expected_result: A click from prompt B matches only B and only B can reach deleteBot.
reproduction.observed_result: One synthetic click matched collector targets A and B. With single acknowledgment modeled, target A deleted before the second execution rejected; the static filters contain no message binding.
reproduction.poc_constraints: BotManager deletion was a local stub; no Discord message, API interaction, database, or bot was created.

findings.existing_controls: The command is ephemeral, resolveAuthorizedBot scopes the target, and BotManager requires the bot be stopped. These prevent foreign deletion but cannot recover user intent when the same authorized user has two dialogs.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Generate a fresh nonce per dialog, include it in the custom IDs/state, fetch/bind the specific reply message, and require both nonce and i.message.id match before using the stored target. Disable only the matched prompt on completion/timeout.
alternatives: Use a message-specific component collector created from the confirmation reply.
Store pending confirmation state keyed by interaction/message ID with one-time consume semantics.
regression_tests: Open two dialogs for one user/channel; click each prompt and assert only its target is deleted.
Assert stale/replayed/foreign-message/nonced component interactions are ignored.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: One click can be consumed by exactly one matching dialog and cannot select a target other than the displayed prompt.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Discord component lifecycle/ephemeral reply APIs require careful UX and acknowledgment handling.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The production filter demonstrably returns true for both synthetic collectors because it omits message/nonce. Discord may reject a second deferUpdate, but that only decides which collector wins; it does not restore binding to the clicked prompt.
findings.limitations: No real Discord gateway was used, so exact collector callback ordering is library/runtime-dependent; the missing binding and unsafe outcome are deterministic.

findings.title: Remote PostgreSQL hostnames beginning with 127. are misclassified as loopback and permitted without TLS
findings.root_cause: Loopback detection applies a textual /^127\./ prefix to any hostname rather than first determining whether it is an IP literal. A remote DNS hostname that starts with those characters is treated as local, so buildSslConfig does not require DB_SSL, rejectUnauthorized, or a CA.
findings.violated_invariant: Only an actual local loopback address/socket may use plaintext PostgreSQL; every remote hostname must require verified TLS.
findings.data_flow: DATABASE_URL/PGHOST -> parseDatabaseTarget URL hostname -> isLoopbackDatabaseHost textual prefix -> remote=false -> buildSslConfig permits undefined ssl -> pg Pool constructed for remote DNS target.
attack_scenario: An operator uses a valid remote database DNS name that happens to begin with the loopback-looking prefix, or a configuration/DNS value is substituted with such a hostname.
The intended remote TLS policy is skipped, even if no explicit DB_SSL settings were supplied.
Database credentials/queries travel without the expected authenticated TLS protection and an on-path actor can observe or modify them.
findings.attacker_role: On-path actor affecting a plaintext remote database connection; configuration/DNS compromise is a prerequisite rather than an unauthenticated web attacker.
findings.preconditions: A remote hostname beginning with the textual loopback prefix is configured, and TLS is not independently forced by environmental settings.
findings.affected_deployment: Remote PostgreSQL deployments with a matching hostname or compromised configuration.

impact.confidentiality: Database credentials and application data may be exposed on the network.
impact.integrity: Database traffic can be altered by an on-path actor.
impact.availability: Traffic interference can disrupt startup and persistence.
impact.blast_radius: All bot records, tokens, and activity data in the connected database.
impact.business_impact: Breaks the documented verified-TLS guarantee for a remote database under a plausible naming/configuration edge case.

reproduction.type: local module-construction proof with a stub pg Pool
steps: Supplied an audit-only remote-shaped PostgreSQL URL whose hostname begins with the loopback prefix; no real endpoint was used.
Replaced pg.Pool with a local capture class before requiring the database module.
Inspected captured options without printing the connection string.
reproduction.expected_result: Remote target construction fails without verified TLS configuration.
reproduction.poc_constraints: The Pool was a local EventEmitter stub; no DNS, TCP, TLS, query, credential, or external service was contacted.

findings.existing_controls: Normal remote hostnames require DB_SSL=true, DB_SSL_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=true, and a validated CA; URL TLS override parameters are rejected. Tests cover ordinary remote/local values but not this lookalike hostname.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Normalize brackets, then use net.isIP and exact parsed CIDR/address comparison for 127.0.0.0/8 and ::1. Treat all non-IP hostnames (including localhost unless explicitly justified) as remote or resolve/restrict them safely before allowing plaintext.
alternatives: Require verified TLS for every TCP database connection and use a Unix socket for explicit local development.
Require an explicit LOCAL_DB_PLAINTEXT=true development-only opt-in.
regression_tests: Assert loopback literals pass only exact/range parsing.
Assert remote names beginning with loopback text fail absent TLS.
Assert URL and discrete PGHOST paths behave identically.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No DNS hostname can disable the remote verified-TLS requirement based on a textual prefix.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Replacing textual detection with parsed address logic is localized and has isolated configuration tests.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The URL parser returns the hostname as a DNS name, not an IPv4 literal. The local capture showed the production condition selected undefined ssl; no claim is made that an arbitrary operator normally uses this naming pattern.
findings.limitations: No remote database or network MITM was contacted; the consequence follows directly from captured pg options and documented PostgreSQL TLS semantics.

findings.title: CSRF Origin fallback accepts a different scheme/port whenever Fetch Metadata is absent
findings.root_cause: When Sec-Fetch-Site is absent, the fallback compares only hostname and deliberately strips the request port; it does not compare URL origin/scheme/port against a configured public origin. Browser cookies are host-scoped rather than port-scoped, so an attacker-controlled same-host alternate HTTPS origin can be cross-origin while passing this check.
findings.violated_invariant: Unsafe cookie-authenticated API requests must be accepted only from the exact dashboard origin, not merely an equal hostname.
findings.data_flow: Unsafe /api browser request with no Fetch Metadata -> Origin header -> sameOriginGuard hostname-only comparison -> authenticated cookie route -> BotManager/token mutation sink.
attack_scenario: A deployment has an untrusted/compromised app or tenant reachable at a different HTTPS port on the dashboard hostname, and a browser does not provide Fetch Metadata.
That origin sends an unsafe request to the dashboard origin. The host-only cookie can accompany a same-host request.
Its Origin has the same hostname but different port/scheme; guard accepts it and a valid cookie allows the requested bot/token mutation.
findings.attacker_role: Actor controlling another origin on the same hostname, under a browser/client path without Sec-Fetch-Site.
findings.preconditions: Same hostname with a distinct attacker-controlled origin, valid session cookie, and absent Fetch Metadata. Modern clients that send same-site/cross-site Fetch Metadata are blocked.
findings.affected_deployment: Multi-service/alternate-port public deployments and legacy/non-Fetch-Metadata browser paths.

impact.confidentiality: May expose mutation results/readable same-origin API effects depending on browser CORS and endpoint behavior.
impact.integrity: Can drive authenticated bot start/stop/edit/delete or token-management mutations.
impact.availability: Can delete/stop bots through a forged unsafe request.
impact.blast_radius: Resources accessible to the victim session.
impact.business_impact: Defense-in-depth CSRF protection fails in a conditional but realistic shared-host topology.

reproduction.type: local loopback HTTP server test; no external connection
steps: Started createWebApp on a temporary 127.0.0.1 port with audit-only configuration.
Sent POST /api/auth/logout with no Sec-Fetch-Site and an Origin with the same hostname but a different HTTPS scheme/port.
Sent a different-host Origin control request.
reproduction.expected_result: Different scheme/port Origin is rejected with 403.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Local server only, no authentication token/cookie, no database call, and no real service contact.

findings.existing_controls: SameSite=Lax cookie, JSON parsing, Fetch Metadata rejection when present, global/API rate limits, and server-side authorization reduce exploitation. Existing tests cover only same-host exact origin and different host, not different scheme/port.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Add a configured canonical WEB_PUBLIC_ORIGIN for public deployments and compare new URL(Origin).origin exactly against it (including scheme/port). For unsafe cookie-authenticated requests, require exact Origin or a CSRF token/custom-header policy rather than trusting absence wholesale.
alternatives: Use synchronizer/double-submit CSRF tokens on all unsafe session-cookie routes.
Allow non-browser clients through a separate bearer-token API rather than an Origin-less cookie fallback.
regression_tests: Assert equal host/different port and equal host/different scheme receive 403 without Fetch Metadata.
Assert configured canonical origin succeeds and no-Origin API policy behaves as designed.
Exercise a cookie-bearing mutation route under the same setup.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No cross-origin URL can pass solely because its hostname matches the request host.

findings.auto_fix_reason: A canonical public origin and non-browser client policy change deployment/API behavior and needs documentation/migration review.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The status code was observed from the actual middleware. Severity is conditional because modern Fetch Metadata is checked first and an attacker needs another same-host origin; this is not claimed as a universal cross-site bypass.
findings.limitations: The local request did not carry a real browser cookie and did not emulate legacy-browser Fetch Metadata behavior; it proves the guard acceptance condition only.

findings.title: Docker runtime image accepts unreviewed build-context artifacts after trusted build output
findings.owasp: A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures
findings.excerpt:
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=web-build /app/web/dist ./web/dist
COPY . .
// .dockerignore does not exclude web/dist or common local credential files
findings.root_cause: The runtime stage copies reviewed builder output and then overlays the entire Docker context. .dockerignore does not exclude Git-ignored web/dist, so a pre-existing artifact can replace the builder output. The broad context copy also permits non-excluded local credential files (for example common package-manager credentials or environment variants) into image layers.
findings.violated_invariant: The runtime image must contain only explicitly selected, reviewed build outputs and must never inherit arbitrary untracked workstation/CI artifacts or secrets.
findings.data_flow: Developer/CI workspace untracked or ignored file -> Docker build context (not matched by .dockerignore) -> final COPY . . -> /app runtime filesystem; web/dist is served by Express as same-origin dashboard assets.
attack_scenario: A developer/CI workspace contains stale or attacker-modified ignored frontend output before docker build.
The builder creates a clean frontend, but final COPY overlays it with the workspace version.
The image serves unreviewed same-origin JavaScript, which can perform authenticated API actions in a user browser; similarly, non-excluded local credentials can persist in image layers.
findings.attacker_role: Local workstation/CI workspace attacker, malicious build artifact producer, or operator who builds from an unclean directory.
findings.preconditions: Docker image is built from an unclean/attacker-influenced workspace containing a file not excluded by .dockerignore. No current live secret was found in tracked files.
findings.affected_deployment: Local or CI Docker builds using the repository root as context.

impact.confidentiality: Local build secrets can be embedded in image layers and malicious frontend code can exfiltrate same-origin API data.
impact.integrity: Stale/malicious dashboard JavaScript can replace the intended builder output.
impact.availability: Bad artifacts can break the dashboard or send destructive authenticated API calls.
impact.blast_radius: Every deployment/browser receiving the produced image.
impact.business_impact: A workstation/CI compromise becomes a production dashboard integrity and credential-exposure path.

reproduction.type: static Docker build-context proof; Docker daemon intentionally not used
steps: Compared Git ignore rules with .dockerignore and confirmed web/dist is Git-ignored but absent from Docker exclusions.
Traced Dockerfile ordering: builder dist copy precedes broad final COPY . . .
Built the frontend locally only to inspect generated static structure; no Docker image or external service was built/contacted.
reproduction.expected_result: Final stage copies only explicit source/runtime files and cannot overwrite builder dist from context.
reproduction.observed_result: The static ordering permits context web/dist overlay; .dockerignore excludes .env but not web/dist or all common credential patterns.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No malicious artifact, secret, Docker image, registry, or production system was created or used.

findings.existing_controls: Multi-stage build, npm lockfiles, non-root runtime, read-only root filesystem, and .dockerignore exclusions for .env/.git/logs are positive controls. They do not constrain the final broad context overlay.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Add web/dist and broad credential/build-artifact patterns to .dockerignore, then replace COPY . . with explicit allowlisted COPY instructions for runtime source/package files. Copy only builder-owned dist into final image.
alternatives: Build from a clean exported source tree in CI.
Pin base image digest, use npm ci --ignore-scripts only after compatibility review, generate SBOM/provenance, and scan image layers.
regression_tests: Build from a temporary context containing a sentinel web/dist file and assert it is absent/replaced in final image.
Assert sentinel credential filenames are excluded from context/image.
Run docker build --no-cache and application health smoke test in an environment with Docker.
verification_commands: docker build --no-cache . (not available in this sandbox)
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No untracked context file can overwrite built assets or appear in the runtime filesystem unless explicitly allowlisted.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Changing COPY allowlists/.dockerignore must be validated against all intended runtime files and production image behavior.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The bug is conditional on unclean context; it is not claimed that the audited generated web/dist is malicious. Docker COPY overlay semantics and the observed ignore mismatch make the integrity boundary objectively absent.
findings.limitations: Docker daemon is unavailable, so no image-layer integration test ran. No untracked secret file was created for the audit.

findings.title: Deployment guide presents Cloudflare Flexible TLS as a short-term setup for JWT-bearing controls
findings.symbol: Recommended Cloudflare setup and long-term setup
findings.excerpt:
The short-term setup is: ... choose Flexible only when the origin cannot support TLS.
Flexible encrypts visitor-to-edge traffic while edge-to-origin remains HTTP.
...
Because this dashboard handles JWT-backed login and bot controls, treat Flexible as temporary.
findings.root_cause: The guide labels a mode with a plaintext edge-to-origin hop as a recommended short-term setup for a session-bearing administration surface. It warns about the risk and later recommends Full (strict), but does not make encrypted origin transport/isolation a prerequisite before public use.
findings.violated_invariant: Public dashboard session cookies and bot-control requests should remain confidential and tamper-resistant across every untrusted network hop.
findings.data_flow: Browser HTTPS -> Cloudflare edge TLS -> Flexible mode HTTP origin hop -> Node HTTP listener -> dashboard cookie/API/SSE. The application cannot itself add TLS when WEB_HTTPS=true.
attack_scenario: An operator follows the short-term Flexible instructions while the origin path traverses an untrusted/shared network.
A network actor between edge and origin observes or modifies requests/responses containing authenticated dashboard traffic.
The actor can steal/replay session-bearing requests or alter bot-control responses until the deployment moves to verified origin TLS.
findings.attacker_role: Network actor on the Cloudflare-to-origin path.
findings.preconditions: A public deployment follows Flexible-mode guidance and the edge-origin path is not fully trusted/isolated.
findings.affected_deployment: Only Flexible TLS deployments; actual Cloudflare configuration was not available and was not contacted.

impact.confidentiality: JWT session traffic can be observed on the plaintext origin hop.
impact.integrity: Responses/requests can be modified in transit.
impact.availability: An on-path actor can disrupt traffic.
impact.blast_radius: All dashboard users and bot controls transiting the affected origin path.
impact.business_impact: Documentation can lead to deployment of a privileged control plane without end-to-end transport protection.

steps: Read the relevant Cloudflare guide sections and the application server TLS behavior.
Confirmed server uses HTTP and WEB_HTTPS only changes browser headers/cookie flags; it does not create a TLS listener.
reproduction.expected_result: Public deployment instructions require a verified encrypted origin hop or explicitly restrict any exception to an isolated trusted network with no privileged traffic.
reproduction.observed_result: The guide calls Flexible a short-term setup while explicitly stating the origin hop remains HTTP.

These reduce but do not eliminate the hazardous recommendation.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Reframe Flexible as a non-production emergency exception, require an isolated trusted origin network and a dated migration plan, and make Full (strict) with origin certificate/proxy TLS the only recommended public deployment path.
alternatives: Remove Flexible instructions entirely from the privileged-dashboard guide.
Add startup/deployment preflight documentation that rejects public exposure until verified origin TLS is configured.
regression_tests: Documentation review checklist asserting public examples state Full (strict) and origin isolation.
In a safe staging environment, verify end-to-end TLS and cookie/header behavior without exposing a real control plane.
verification_commands: manual deployment review (not run; no cloud contact permitted)
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No public deployment path is described as recommended if its origin hop carries privileged session/control traffic in plaintext.
